newsitem.title: THAILAND: Somprasong default seen renewing property fears.
newsitem.headline: Somprasong default seen renewing property fears.

text.p: A Eurobond debt default by listed Thai developer Somprasong Land Plc, is likely to intensify concerns surrounding the stability of some Thai property companies and their creditors, analysts said.
Somprasong became the first Thai company to default on a Euroconvertible debenture (ECD) interest payment on Tuesday when it failed to honour a $3.1 million debt due on its $80 million ECD issue.

"There have been repeated rumours on property companies and I think it could now spread to those finance firms which have high loan exposure to property," said a fixed income researcher at Swiss Bank Corporation.

Finance companies have an average 25 percent of their loans in the property sector, though some have exposure running at 40 percent. The Somprasong default may now revive worries about the loan portfolio quality of some finance firms, analysts said.

"In my opinion I think this will renew concerns about the level of non-performing loans among finance companies, though there are other factors affecting that too, such as rates of economic growth," said an analyst at Thai Farmers Bank Research Centre.
Somprasong's failure to meet the payment deadline surprised analysts in Thailand where financial backers have traditionally assisted troubled companies.

The Thai SET Index languished at its 54-month low on Thursday, mainly on persistent market concern about steady depreciation of the Thai baht against the dollar in the past few months and positions of banks and financial firms with large loan exposure to the ailing property sector.

The stock market has also been hurt by soaring short-term interest rates in the past two weeks. The Bank of Thailand has tried to keep interest rates high to stem an outflow of funds as foreign investors try to trim foreign exchange losses by switching baht-denominated assets into those kept in dollar.
"There now doesn't seem to be anything stopping this happening to some other property companies in the future given the difficulties," said the researcher.

That propsect is likely to dampen investor sentiment towards Thailand, which has already been affected by a current account deficit estimated at 8.2 percent of GDP in 1996, static export growth last year, and sporadic attacks on the currency.

"Foreign investors may perceive the overall risk of investment in Thailand to be higher now, though there is a possibility that this (default) will be considered an isolated case," said the Thai Farmers analyst.
Whether Somprasong remains an isolated case depends on whether other Thai property firms can weather a protracted slump in the Thai property market, analysts said.
The Bank of Thailand, which is co-ordinating efforts to revive the market, recently estimated oversupply in Bangkok and its environs at 350,000 units at the end of 1996.
High domestic prime interest rate, at over 13 percent, have stunted demand and increased developers' financing costs, analysts said.
Even with government efforts under way to boost the market, optimistic estimates reckon it could still take two to three years for the sector to recover, analysts said.
